title: EvalStructure: Abstract Model of Universal Computation
content: EvalStructure is a minimal type-theoretic model of computation: a triple (Ob, Val, eval) where Ob represents programs/codes, Val represents output values, and eval : Ob → Ob → Val is the evaluation function. IsPointSurjective requires that every function Ob → Val is 'represented' by some code—formally, ∀ g : Ob → Val, ∃ a : Ob, ∀ x : Ob, eval a x = g x. This is exactly the property of a universal Turing machine. The abstraction separates universality from any specific computational model (Turing machines, lambda calculus, partial recursive functions), making subsequent results model-independent.
mathContext: In categorical terms: an EvalStructure is a set $A$ with a 'point-surjective' map $A \to B^A$ (the exponential), where $B = $ Val. Point-surjectivity: $\forall g \in B^A, \exists a \in A$ such that $\text{eval}(a, -) = g$. This formalizes universality: every function $A \to B$ is computable by some program in $A$.
prerequisites: function types in dependent type theory

title: Lawvere Fixed-Point Theorem: The Diagonal Argument Abstracted
content: lawvere_fpt is the abstract diagonal argument: if E is point-surjective, every endomorphism f : Val → Val has a fixed point. The proof is a one-liner: obtain the code a₀ representing the diagonal function x ↦ f(eval x x); then eval a₀ a₀ is a fixed point. The proof reads: obtain ⟨a₀, ha₀⟩ := hE (fun a => f (E.eval a a)); exact ⟨E.eval a₀ a₀, (ha₀ a₀).symm⟩. This single theorem simultaneously captures Cantor's diagonal argument, Gödel's diagonalization lemma, Turing's self-application, and the Y-combinator in one 2-line Lean proof.
mathContext: The Lawvere diagonal: given point-surjective $e: A \to B^A$, for $f: B \to B$, define $d(a) = f(e(a)(a))$. By point-surjectivity, $\exists a_0: e(a_0) = d$. Then $e(a_0)(a_0) = d(a_0) = f(e(a_0)(a_0))$, giving fixed point $v = e(a_0)(a_0)$.

title: Abstract Rice: Bool.not Has No Fixed Point → No Universal Bool Evaluation
content: abstract_rice proves that no eval : A → A → Bool can be point-surjective, by contradiction: assume point-surjectivity, apply lawvere_fpt with f = (! ·), get ⟨v, hv : !v = v⟩, then cases v <;> simp_all produces contradiction (both Bool cases fail). This is Rice's theorem in its Lawvere form: Bool.not is the universal obstruction to decidable universality. rice_induced_obstruction extends this: even if the underlying computation is universal over a richer value type V, composing with any d : V → Bool cannot make the Boolean classification universal. rice_undecidable_witness provides the concrete witness: ∃ f : A → Bool that eval e cannot represent, for any e.

title: Semantic Properties and Flip Programs: Contradiction Without Surjectivity
content: SemanticProperty formalizes Rice's extensionality condition: P(a) depends only on the behavior of a (eval a x for all x), not the syntax of a. HasFlipProgram formalizes non-triviality: a code transformer flip with P(flip a) ≠ P(a) for all a. semantic_rice_flip is the cleanest Rice argument: if flip preserves semantics (eval(flip a, x) = eval(a, x)) but flips property (P(flip a) ≠ P(a)), then hP_sem gives P(flip a) = P(a) (same behavior → same property), directly contradicting h_flip_prop. No Lawvere or point-surjectivity is needed—just the definitions of semantic and flip. The Nonempty constraint allows Classical.arbitrary to obtain a witness.
mathContext: A semantic $P$ satisfies: $\text{eval}(a,x) = \text{eval}(b,x) \forall x \implies P(a) = P(b)$. A flip satisfies: $\text{eval}(\text{flip}(a), x) = \text{eval}(a, x) \forall x$ (semantics-preserving) but $P(\text{flip}(a)) \neq P(a)$ (property-flipping). The two conditions together: $P(\text{flip}(a)) = P(a)$ (by semantic) and $P(\text{flip}(a)) \neq P(a)$ (by flip). Contradiction.

title: HaltingModel: Turing's Undecidability as a Rice Corollary
content: HaltingModel axiomatizes a decidable halting predicate with universal machine: Prog is the (unified) type of programs and inputs (standard via Gödel coding), halts : Prog → Prog → Bool is the purported decidable halting function, and universal asserts every Bool-valued function is represented by halts e for some e. no_halting_model proves this model is impossible (False) in one line: exact abstract_rice M.Prog M.halts M.universal. The M.universal field is definitionally IsPointSurjective of the halting structure, so abstract_rice applies. This derives Turing's 1936 halting problem undecidability as a one-line corollary of the Lawvere framework.
mathContext: Turing's theorem: $\nexists h: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \{0,1\}$ such that $h(e, x) = 1 \iff \varphi_e(x)\downarrow$ and $\forall f: \mathbb{N} \to \{0,1\}, \exists e: \forall x, h(e,x) = f(x)$ (universality). Universality is point-surjectivity of $(\mathbb{N}, \text{Bool}, h)$; abstract_rice forbids this.

title: Classical Rice via Kleene Recursion: The Flipper Fixed-Point Argument
content: classical_rice_abstract uses ClassicalRiceModel which axiomatizes Kleene's recursion theorem: every code transformer f : Code → Code has a semantic fixed point e* with semantics(f(e*)) = semantics(e*). The proof defines the flipper f(e) = if P(e) = true then e₀ else e₁ (swapping which non-trivial behavior is targeted). Kleene gives e* with semantics(f(e*)) = semantics(e*). Since P is semantic: P(e*) = P(f(e*)) (same semantics → same property). But f was designed to flip P: split_ifs with h + simp [hP₀/hP₁] shows P(f(e*)) ≠ P(e*) in both Bool cases. Contradiction. The Bool.eq_false_iff handles the case when P e_star ≠ true.
mathContext: **Kleene's recursion theorem**: $\forall f: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}, \exists e^*: \varphi_{f(e^*)} = \varphi_{e^*}$ (a Lawvere fixed point in the extensional evaluation structure). **Rice (classical)**: If $P$ is semantic and non-trivial ($\exists e_0: P(e_0) = 0$, $\exists e_1: P(e_1) = 1$), the flipper $F(e) = e_0$ if $P(e) = 1$, $e_1$ if $P(e) = 0$ flips $P$. Kleene gives $e^*$ with $\varphi_{F(e^*)} = \varphi_{e^*}$, so $P(F(e^*)) = P(e^*)$ (semantic). But $P(F(e^*)) \neq P(e^*)$ by design. Contradiction.
